content_html:
Financial ratios turn the raw numbers in a company's financial statements into measures you can compare across years or with similar businesses. This calculator takes figures from one year's income statement and the balance sheet at the end of that year and calculates 16 common ratios in four groups: liquidity, profitability, leverage and efficiency.

How to use this calculator

  1. Income statement: enter revenue, cost of goods sold, operating expenses, interest expense, any other income (negative for other losses) and income taxes for the year.
  2. Balance sheet: enter cash, accounts receivable, inventory, total current assets, total assets, total current liabilities and total liabilities as of the end of the year.
  3. The calculator works out gross profit, operating income, net income, shareholders' equity (total assets minus total liabilities) and working capital, then every ratio.

Use the same period and the same units for every figure. If a business has no inventory, such as most service firms, enter 0; inventory ratios then show "n/a."

What the ratios measure

Liquidity

The current, quick and cash ratios compare short-term assets with debts due within a year. The quick ratio leaves out inventory, which may take time to sell, and the cash ratio counts only cash. A result above 1 means those assets exceed short-term debts.

Profitability

Gross, operating and net margins show how much of each sales dollar remains after production costs, after running costs and after everything including interest and tax. Return on assets and return on equity relate net income to what the business owns and to what the owners have invested.

Leverage

Debt-to-equity and the debt ratio show how much of the business is financed by creditors rather than owners. Interest coverage shows how many times operating income covers interest expense.

Efficiency

Asset turnover measures sales generated per dollar of assets. Inventory turnover and days inventory outstanding show how quickly stock sells, and receivables turnover and days sales outstanding show how quickly customers pay.

A worked example

The default figures describe a business with $1,000,000 of revenue, $600,000 cost of goods sold and $250,000 operating expenses. Gross profit is $400,000 (a 40.0% margin) and operating income is $150,000 (15.0%). After $20,000 interest and $30,000 tax, net income is $100,000, a 10.0% net margin.

Reading the results sensibly

  • Compare like with like. A healthy ratio for a grocery chain looks very different from one for a software company, so compare with businesses in the same industry.
  • Look at trends. Calculating the same ratios for several years often says more than a single year.
  • Remember the shortcuts. This calculator uses end-of-year balances. Many analysts use the average of the opening and closing balance for turnover and return ratios, which can give somewhat different results for a fast-growing business.
  • Negative equity makes return on equity and debt-to-equity meaningless, so the calculator shows "n/a" for them.

faq.question: What is a good current ratio?
faq.answer: It depends on the industry. Many analysts view a current ratio between about 1.2 and 2 as comfortable, but businesses with fast-moving inventory or steady cash sales can operate safely with less. Compare with similar companies rather than relying on one rule of thumb.

faq.question: What is the difference between ROA and ROE?
faq.answer: Return on assets divides net income by everything the business owns, while return on equity divides it only by the owners' stake. Debt raises ROE relative to ROA, so a high ROE can reflect strong profits, heavy borrowing or both.

faq.question: Where do I find the numbers for this calculator?
faq.answer: Revenue, cost of goods sold, operating expenses, interest and taxes come from the income statement. Cash, receivables, inventory, assets and liabilities come from the balance sheet. Public companies publish both in their annual reports.

faq.question: Why does a ratio show n/a?
faq.answer: A ratio can't be calculated when its denominator is zero, for example interest coverage with no interest expense or inventory turnover with no inventory. Return on equity and debt-to-equity also show n/a when equity is zero or negative.

faq.question: Should I use year-end or average balances?
faq.answer: This calculator uses the balances you enter, usually year-end figures. For turnover and return ratios, many analysts average the opening and closing balances; you can do the same by entering those averages instead.
